name: Fournier gangrene
aliases: necrotising fasciitis of the perineum and genitalia

clinicalPearls: Fournier gangrene is a rapidly progressive, life-threatening necrotising fasciitis of the perineal, genital, and perianal region, most often affecting men but also occurring in women

It is typically polymicrobial and synergistic, involving a mixture of aerobic and anaerobic organisms (such as coliforms, streptococci, staphylococci, and anaerobes like Bacteroides and Clostridium) arising from anorectal, genitourinary, or cutaneous sources
Diabetes mellitus is the commonest predisposing condition, and other forms of immunosuppression, alcohol excess, obesity, and local trauma increase risk

Early signs (severe pain out of proportion to visible findings, oedema, and erythema) can be deceptively subtle before crepitus, skin discolouration, bullae, foul-smelling discharge, and frank necrosis develop
Systemic toxicity and sepsis frequently outpace the visible skin changes because the infection tracks rapidly along fascial planes beneath apparently viable skin
It is a clinical diagnosis and a surgical emergency; imaging (showing soft-tissue gas or fascial fluid) must not delay treatment when suspicion is high
Management combines aggressive fluid resuscitation, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and, above all, urgent and often repeated surgical debridement of all necrotic tissue
Diversion (urinary or faecal), reconstructive surgery, and adjuncts such as hyperbaric oxygen may be considered, and severity scoring helps gauge prognosis
reference.pathophysiology: Fournier gangrene begins when organisms breach the perineal, genital, or perianal tissues, commonly from an anorectal abscess or fistula, a urogenital infection or instrumentation, or a skin breach. A synergistic mix of aerobic and anaerobic bacteria then proliferates, the aerobes promoting anaerobic growth by consuming oxygen and impairing host defences while the combined enzymatic activity (including collagenases, hyaluronidases, and other exotoxins) digests fascia and connective tissue. The infection spreads rapidly along the relatively avascular fascial planes, and an obliterative endarteritis of subcutaneous vessels produces ischaemic necrosis of the overlying skin, gas formation, and the release of toxins that drive a systemic inflammatory response and septic shock. Impaired host defences, as in diabetes and other immunosuppressed states, accelerate this process.
additionalDifferentials: Severe cellulitis or a simple perineal or scrotal abscess
Perianal or ischiorectal abscess without necrotising spread
Pyoderma gangrenosum or another necrotising dermatosis
Gas gangrene (clostridial myonecrosis) of adjacent tissues
additionalInvestigations: Blood cultures and tissue or wound cultures (aerobic and anaerobic) to guide antimicrobial therapy
Full blood count, renal and liver function, glucose, lactate, and inflammatory markers, with severity scoring where used
Coagulation studies and group-and-save in anticipation of surgery
Bedside or cross-sectional imaging (ultrasound, plain radiograph, or CT) to detect soft-tissue gas and fascial fluid without delaying surgery
Assessment for underlying diabetes or other immunocompromise
Intraoperative tissue sampling and histology to confirm necrotising fasciitis and identify the source
redFlags: Pain markedly out of proportion to visible skin findings
Crepitus, skin discolouration or bullae, and foul-smelling discharge indicating advancing necrosis
Systemic features of sepsis or septic shock such as hypotension, tachycardia, and confusion
Rapid progression of erythema or induration over hours
Any diagnostic delay, as mortality rises sharply without prompt debridement
reference.prognosis: Fournier gangrene carries a substantial mortality that rises steeply with delayed surgery, extensive disease, and severe sepsis; early aggressive debridement with intensive supportive care markedly improves survival, though survivors may face major tissue loss requiring reconstruction and long rehabilitation.
pitfalls: Underestimating early disease because the skin looks relatively benign while infection spreads along deeper fascial planes
Delaying surgical debridement to await imaging or a microbiological result
Relying on antibiotics alone without adequate and repeated surgical exploration
Performing insufficiently extensive initial debridement and not planning early re-look surgery
Failing to identify and control the source and to treat underlying diabetes or immunosuppression
references: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
IDSA guidelines for the diagnosis and management of skin and soft tissue infections
European Association of Urology guidance on urological infections
management: Immediate, wide surgical debridement of all necrotic tissue with repeated re-exploration and source control is the life-saving mainstay
Start broad-spectrum empirical antibiotics covering Gram-positive, Gram-negative and anaerobic organisms, adding clindamycin for its antitoxin effect, then de-escalate to culture results
Resuscitate aggressively for sepsis with intravenous fluids, vasopressors and organ support in a critical care setting
Optimise glycaemic control and treat the underlying diabetes or other immunocompromise
Divert the faecal or urinary stream, for example with a defunctioning colostomy or suprapubic catheter, where perineal contamination threatens the wound
Provide nutritional support and consider adjunctive hyperbaric oxygen where available
Plan staged reconstructive surgery once sepsis resolves, coordinated through a multidisciplinary surgical team
